 The Maximum SSI Payment Is Rising in 2027 - But There’s a Catch
 Jordan Major 2026년 11월 16일 월 오후 1:23 UTC 0 
Millions of Supplemental Security Income (SSI) recipients are getting a raise in 2027, with the maximum federal payment climbing above $1,000 a month for the first time.
The Social Security Administration (SSA) announced a 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) on October 14, raising the maximum federal SSI payment from $994 to $1,029 a month. While the increase could provide some relief if you're living on just Social Security , not everyone will receive the full amount.

 The maximum SSI payment will rise to $1,029
The 3.6% COLA means eligible individuals could receive up to $35 more each month, or $420 annually. Eligible couples will also see their maximum rise from $1,491 to $1,544 a month, an increase of $53 monthly or up to $636 over a year.
"Social Security will implement this cost-of-living adjustment for 76 million Americans, giving them greater financial stability," Social Security Commissioner Frank J. Bisignano said when announcing the increase.
Around 7.3 million people receive SSI, according to the SSA. Their higher payments will begin on December 31, 2026, because January 1 is a federal holiday. However, receiving SSI doesn't automatically qualify you for the new $1,029 maximum.

 Your income can reduce your SSI payment
SSI is designed for people with limited income and resources who are 65 or older, blind, or have a qualifying disability. The amount you receive depends partly on your countable income.
To calculate your federal SSI payment, SSA starts with the federal benefit rate and subtracts countable income. Not all income counts, and earned and unearned income are treated differently.
SSA typically excludes the first $20 of most income each month, plus the first $65 of wages and half of any additional earnings. As a result, SSI generally falls by about $1 for every $2 earned from work after applicable exclusions. By comparison, each $1 of countable non-work income can reduce SSI by $1.
Social Security benefits, pensions, unemployment benefits, interest, and dividends are among the types of unearned income that can potentially affect your payment.
 Where and how you live can affect your SSI payment 
Income isn't the only reason someone could receive less than $1,029. Your living arrangement could also affect your SSI payment, particularly if someone else helps cover your shelter expenses.
If you live in another person's home without paying your share of certain costs, SSA may count that assistance as income, potentially reducing your benefit.

There has been one important recent change to these rules. Since September 30, 2024, food provided by other people no longer counts as in-kind support and maintenance. Shelter assistance, however, can still affect benefits.
Income from certain family members can matter as well. SSA may consider some of a spouse's income when determining an adult recipient's SSI benefit. A parent's income can affect benefits for an eligible child living at home. 
 The result is that two people who both qualify for SSI could receive different monthly amounts even though the federal maximum is the same.

 The $2,000 resource limit isn't increasing
There's another number SSI recipients should pay attention to in the SSA's 2027 announcement. While the maximum federal payment is rising 3.6%, the SSI resource limits aren't changing. They remain $2,000 for an individual and $3,000 for a couple in 2027.
Resources can include money in checking and savings accounts, cash, stocks, bonds, and certain other assets you own.
Not everything counts toward the limit. The home you live in and generally one vehicle used by you or a member of your household for transportation are among the resources SSA doesn't count.
Even with higher monthly payments, accumulating more than $2,000 in countable resources could put an individual's SSI eligibility at risk.
 Some recipients could receive more than $1,029
The federal maximum isn't necessarily the absolute most an SSI recipient can receive either. Some states supplement the federal SSI benefit with additional payments. Depending on where you live and your circumstances, your combined federal and state benefit could therefore exceed $1,029.
Your personal COLA notice should show what you'll actually receive rather than simply the maximum federal amount announced by SSA.
Most recipients who have a my Social Security account and have opted for paperless notices can view their COLA notice in the online Message Center starting in late November. SSA will mail notices in December to those who haven't enrolled in paperless notices.
 Bottom line
The maximum federal SSI payment will rise to $1,029 monthly for individuals and $1,544 for eligible couples in 2027. However, your actual benefit may be lower depending on your income and living arrangements.
And while payments are increasing, SSI's resource limits remain unchanged at $2,000 for individuals and $3,000 for couples. The higher payments could be welcome when retirement savings are stretched thin , but keeping track of countable assets remains essential to maintaining eligibility.
